FIS in Its Designer’s Words
What Does FIS Mean?

FIS is the name of Dr. Bardia Khosravani’s investing system (Rose educational collection); his video descriptions call it Financial Investing System and his research paper (1405) Fundamental Investing System.
In that paper, FIS is a scoring system: companies get 0 to 100 points on 11 fundamental variables (four “FIS score” lessons in this hall).
Its base is fundamental analysis of Codal reports, not charts.
The goals he states: sustainable, low-risk profit in Iran’s stock market, passive income and early retirement.
These are goals, not guarantees. No method has a guaranteed return.
I have this habit: every day I come and look at Codal
Video “Highlights of the FIS introductory course”, YouTube, Aban 1403, minute 3 (transcript)
Two Kinds of Stock
Dividend-focused: pays out a large part of profit in cash every year; the return comes mostly from the DPS.
Capital-gain-focused (growth-focused): keeps profit and spends it on projects; the return comes mostly from price growth.
Companies’ payout policies range from about 10% to 90% of profit.

Where is the line? In a post on his channel (Mehr 1404) he confirmed this definition: “a company that has above 60% is dividend-focused”; meaning the payout percentage. In his videos he uses a payout above 70% as the benchmark for “good”.
In Iran, FIS prefers dividend-focused stocks.
Why Dividend-Focused in Iran?

According to him, classic theories don’t work well in Iran’s market, because systematic risk (sanctions, currency, government decisions, war) moves the whole market together and doesn’t go away with diversification.
A dividend is money that has reached you and is no longer exposed to that risk.
Repeated dividends confirm accounting profit with money (that is, profit quality).
Dividends received can be reinvested or spent on living.
Where Does This Section Come From?
From Dr. Khosravani’s public teachings: his blog, the 1405 research paper, 42 videos on his Aparat channel, his YouTube videos and his Telegram channel, in this app’s own words.
It doesn’t rewrite his paid courses (such as Master FIS).
His return claims (such as “a return of twice inflation”) are quoted here as claims, not tested facts. The list of sources is in this section’s guidebook.

The Golden Three Formula
Three Conditions
1. Sustainable profit-making: a business that makes operating profit year after year (sustainable profit from the FIS 1 section).
2. A high payout: a large part of profit reaches shareholders in cash.
3. Profit growth above inflation: nominal profit rises faster than inflation, so the real value of the dividend is kept and grows.
Golden Three = sustainable profit + a high payout + profit growth above inflation
The Real Growth Test
Profit growth from 1,000 to 1,400 (40%) with inflation of 30% → 1.4 ÷ 1.3 − 1 ≈ 7.7% real growth; the third condition is met.
Nominal growth of 25% with inflation of 35% means real profit shrank, even if the number looks bigger.
Measure growth with an average of several years, not one peak year.
Real growth = (1 + nominal growth) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1

A high payout: the approved DPS in the ordinary general meeting’s minutes, and the DPS ÷ EPS ratio over several years.
Growth above inflation: EPS and DPS over several years next to those years’ inflation rates.
A high payout funded by borrowing is a red flag, not a golden condition.

The Meeting, Dividend Yield and Other Options
Dividend Yield

Meeting Day and After
On the reopening day after the meeting, theoretical price = previous price − DPS. Money moves from one of your pockets to the other and wealth doesn’t change.
The payment deadline is 8 months after the meeting, and small shareholders are usually paid sooner (see the payment schedule on Codal).
Dr. Khosravani’s argument: if next year’s DPS is bigger, the price reaches a higher level at the same dividend yield. So the price recovery depends on profit growth, not on the meeting itself.

The Free Share and the Financial Freedom Formula
What Is a Free Share?
When the total dividends you’ve received equal the money you paid for the share, your capital has come back and the share you still hold is in effect “free” (a free asset).
How fast that happens depends on the dividend yield and DPS growth.
Example: buy 10 million tomans, dividend yield 25% (2.5 million in the first year) and DPS growth 30% → 2.5 + 3.25 + 4.23 ≈ 9.98 million in 3 years; a little over 3 years.
The goal he states: getting your capital back from dividends in about 3 years. That goal needs a high dividend yield and profit growth, and isn’t possible with every stock.
“Free” is an accounting idea: 10 million three years later, with inflation, buys less.
The Financial Freedom Formula
Monthly spending 40 million tomans and a dividend yield of 20% → 40 × 12 ÷ 0.2 = 2,400 million tomans (2.4 billion).
With inflation, spending rises every year; so the DPS must grow at least as fast as inflation (the third condition), or part of the dividend must be reinvested.
Dividends arrive once a year and sometimes late; an emergency fund and a monthly cash plan are needed.
Test claims such as “a return of twice inflation” or “an income five times your salary” against your own numbers and record.
Capital needed = monthly spending × 12 ÷ dividend yield
Shares First, Then Spending
On his channel he tells the story of someone who, from 1396, used his salary at the start of each month to buy a few shares of a dividend-focused company for the long term, and then spent the rest.
The habit matters more than the amount: regular monthly buying, holding, and meeting dividends adding up.
Examples tagged #free_asset on his channel: a cement stock that became “free” in four years, and a sugar stock that became free in 3 years from meeting dividends.
Remember: these are hand-picked examples; there were also stocks that never became free.
Two Lessons from His Own Experience
He sees retiring at 28 as the result of collecting meeting dividends and holding shares.
The biggest mistake he reports of himself: pulling money out of the market to buy a physical asset; that is, switching off the profit-making machine.
“Enjoying is different from owning”: to enjoy a villa you don’t need to lock your capital in a villa.
These are personal experiences; weigh them against your own needs and situation.
Financial Freedom in Five to Seven Years
In introducing the Master FIS course, he gives its target horizon as financial independence and independence of decision in 5 to 7 years.
This is a stated goal, not a guarantee; it depends on how much you save, the real dividend return and inflation.
Test it with this lesson’s formula: write down your yearly spending and see how many years it takes with your own savings and real dividend yield.

Rights Like a Professional
The Share and Its Right
In a capital increase from cash contributions, shareholders have, for each share, the right to buy a new share at the nominal value of 1,000 rials.
The rights symbol is usually the share’s symbol with an “H” at the end (if the symbol is “Alef”: “AlefH”).
During the subscription period (usually 60 days) you either pay the 1,000 rials and get the share, or sell the right in the market.
If you do neither, it is sold under the standard procedure and the money, minus costs, reaches you; usually later and sometimes cheaper (please check).
The Theoretical Value of a Right
Right ≈ share price − 1,000 rials, because by paying 1,000 you get the same share.
After the capital-increase meeting, adjusted price = (P + 1,000 × a) ÷ (1 + a).
The example from his blog: price 6,000 and a 300% increase from contributions → (6,000 + 3 × 1,000) ÷ 4 = 2,250 and right ≈ 1,250.
A shareholder who subscribes is no richer or poorer on the adjustment day: 100 shares × 6,000 + 300,000 paid = 400 shares × 2,250.
Right ≈ share price − 1,000
The Rights Bubble and Dividends
If the old share gets the coming meeting’s DPS but the new share that comes from the right doesn’t, the right is worth less.
Example: share 4,000 and a coming DPS of 500 → fair right ≈ 4,000 − 500 − 1,000 = 2,500. If the right trades at 3,000, it has a bubble of about 500 rials.
Which year’s profit the new share gets is stated in the subscription notice and the meeting minutes on Codal; read the clauses in full (please check).
There is also the time value of money: the 1,000 rials you pay months before the share arrives earns nothing in the meantime.
Fair right ≈ share price − DPS that doesn’t go to the new share − 1,000

Creating Wealth, Industry Margins and Company Size
Creating or Destroying Wealth
From his note on profit margins: net profit must give a return in line with shareholders’ current capital; that is, the market value, not the book value.
And that return must fit the risk (the expected rate of return).
His example: current capital of 1,000 billion tomans and an expected return of 30% → net profit of at least 300 billion. Less than that means destroying wealth.
According to him this condition doesn’t hold in many companies on Iran’s exchange. It is the same comparison of E/P with the expected return as in the FIS 1 section.
If both of these measures hold, the company’s activity will “create wealth” and so “raise the general level of welfare”

Each Industry Has Its Own Margin Norm
A 30% net margin in steel can’t be compared with a distributor’s 3 to 4%.
Judge each company’s margin against its own industry’s average and its own record.
Reasonable net profit margin = minimum profit needed ÷ reasonable sales.
The fact is that the profit margin in each industry has a norm and standard that depends on the nature of that industry

Large (holdings, banks, refineries, petrochemicals): usually less risk.
There is no fixed numerical line; it is measured relative to the whole market.

The FIS-Style Analysis Profile
The Pattern of a Short Analysis
From the analyses he publishes tagged FIS:
1. Industry, main product and by-products.
2. Who sets the product and raw-material prices? (government, commodity exchange, world)
3. Major shareholder and free-float percentage.
4. The multi-year return record (price growth + dividends).
5. Trailing and forward P/E.
6. Forecast assumptions, explicit and written.
7. Sensitivity analysis on the most important assumption.
8. The closing sentence: “This is analysis, not a buy recommendation.”
Purely an analysis, not a recommendation to buy
The end of one of the FIS analyses on the Telegram channel, Tir 1402
Write Down the Assumptions

Sample assumptions for a manufacturer: production = the average of the last 2 years; sales = production; selling and material prices = the latest approved or traded price; by-product share as last year.
An example from one of his analyses: market value 2,850 and forecast profit 650 billion tomans → forward P/E about 4.4.
Sensitivity: recalculate profit with production 30% higher and 30% lower.
Forward P/E = market value ÷ forecast net profit
Scenarios: Which Stock Survives Both Outcomes?
His method for news with two outcomes (for example a deal or no deal): write out each outcome’s effect on the company separately.
A company that profits from a boom in one outcome and from a currency jump in the other (for example, it has positive net foreign-currency assets) carries less scenario risk.
Instead of predicting the news, build the portfolio so it survives both outcomes.

The FIS Score: From 0 to 100
FIS in a Research Paper

In summer 1405, Dr. Khosravani and Saeed Ajorlou published FIS as a scoring system in the journal “Cheshm-andaz-e Hesabdari va Modiriyat” (Accounting and Management Perspective; vol. 9, no. 116, pp. 182 to 197).
The full name in the paper: Fundamental Investing System.
Each company is measured on 11 fundamental variables and gets a score between 0 and 100. A score of 100 means the company got the highest possible points on every variable.

Stepped Points: No Partial Marks
FIS doesn’t multiply each variable by a coefficient. Each variable has several thresholds, and whichever band the variable’s value falls in, it gets that band’s fixed points.
Total score = the sum of the 11 variables’ points.
The effect: the model stays conservative and only rewards companies that fully meet the standard.
The paper hasn’t published the threshold numbers or the points for each step. This app doesn’t guess them either. If you set your own thresholds, call them “my thresholds”, not FIS.
Total score = stepped points of variable 1 + … + stepped points of variable 11
If a company doesn’t pass the next threshold, it doesn’t receive “partial points” for being slightly better.

The Stock Selection Process
1. Exclusion: loss-making companies and companies whose income forecast isn’t reliable get no score at all.
2. Scoring: each company’s 11 variables are calculated from Codal reports and scored.
3. Ranking: from the companies above the market average, the highest are chosen (30 companies in the paper’s test).
4. Price: buy only when the score has reached the minimum needed and the price is also in the buying range (lesson “Entry and exit the FIS way”).
5. Monitoring: with each new financial report the score is recalculated.

The Formulas of the 11 Variables
Forward-Looking Valuation
Forward P/E: the current share price ÷ forecast earnings per share to the end of the financial year.
The forecast in the paper is simple and repeatable: the average monthly profit of the past months of the financial year, extended to the whole year. For example 6-month profit × 2.
Forward P/S: market value ÷ forecast sales to the end of the financial year, with the same monthly-average method.

Earnings expectation gap: the distance between the forward P/E and the trailing P/E (TTM, meaning price ÷ profit of the last 12 months), as a percentage. It shows whether the market expects future profit to grow or fall.

The EPS and P/E that tsetmc shows are trailing. In the video “Getting to know the tsetmc site” (Mordad 1403) he says that EPS is no use for analysis and we must calculate it ourselves from Codal reports.
Earnings expectation gap = |forward P/E − trailing P/E| ÷ trailing P/E × 100
Sales Growth and Profit Margin
Cumulative sales growth: sales of the current period against the same period last year, as a percentage. For example this year’s 6 months against last year’s 6 months.
Profit margin: “FIS profit” ÷ operating income × 100.
“FIS profit” is profit seen conservatively: non-operating or non-recurring income and items are set aside so the picture of sustainable profitability remains.
Profit margin trend growth: this quarter’s profit margin against the previous quarter’s, as a percentage.
Profit margin trend growth = (this quarter’s margin − last quarter’s margin) ÷ last quarter’s margin × 100
The Payout Ratio as FIS Defines It
The paper’s own definition: dividends paid ÷ accumulated profit (not that year’s net profit), for each of the last two years, and the average of the two.
The reason: companies sometimes pay dividends from previous years’ accumulated profit too; this definition shows actual payout behaviour better.
It differs from the usual payout ratio (DPS ÷ EPS) in earlier lessons. When comparing, say which definition you used.
FIS payout ratio = [(last year’s dividends ÷ last year’s accumulated profit) + (this year’s dividends ÷ this year’s accumulated profit)] × 100 ÷ 2
In many cases companies also pay dividends from the accumulated profit of previous years.
Paper text, definition of the payout ratio, p. 186
Receivables, Inventory and the Financial Year
Receivables-to-assets ratio: total receivables ÷ total assets × 100. What share of assets is owed by customers; reliance on credit sales.
Collection period: receivables ÷ total sales × number of days in the period. How many days it takes for sales to turn into cash.
Inventory turnover period: average inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × number of days in the period. How many days it takes goods to turn into money, from arrival to sale.
Financial year: the company’s 12-month reporting period; not necessarily the same as the calendar year. The paper doesn’t say exactly how this variable is scored.

What is clear about the financial year from his videos: he likes companies with different financial years so that dividends arrive each quarter; “the meeting hasn’t been held yet” is on his checklist; and when last year’s meeting hasn’t happened yet, he subtracts the dividend on its way from the market value to see the effective P/E (the Shabandar example in the lesson “Method details 1”). Its exact scoring hasn’t been published.
Collection period = receivables ÷ total sales × days in the period

Entry and Exit the FIS Way
Good Quality, the Right Price
Entering a stock has two conditions: the fundamental score has reached the minimum needed, and the price is in the buying range.

Exit happens in two cases: 1. Fundamental performance has weakened or the quality of financial reports has dropped, and the score has fallen. 2. The price has reached the target valuation range and most of the expected return has been captured.
The portfolio shouldn’t become a single stock. The number of stocks depends on the investor’s own ability to analyse and manage; the paper sets no strict limit.
Quality shares should be bought at the right price and sold at the right price
Paper text, rules for building the portfolio and entry and exit, p. 189
The P/E Range from Akhza
In FIS the right P/E range comes from the risk-free interest rate (Akhza) plus the market risk premium.
The paper’s example: if Akhza is about 40% and the market risk premium is 1 to 1.5 units, the buying P/E range is 3.5 to 4 and the exit range about 7 to 8.
When Akhza changes, the ranges change too. The paper doesn’t give an exact conversion formula; only this example.

P/D: The Ratio He Now Prefers
In his recent videos he says the market looks more at P/D than at P/E.

All of FIS at a Glance: Step by Step
The Full Map, from Codal to Selling
All the pieces of this hall in one seven-step path. We arranged the order, but every step comes from the paper, his videos or his own channel.
1. Preparation: money with a 3 to 7-year horizon, a size below your capacity, no leverage. He himself recommends 6 to 12 months of learning before you start.
2. Screen: loss-makers, companies under Article 141, weak operating margins, adverse or heavily qualified audits, and unpredictable income are set aside.
3. The Golden Three: sustainable profit, a payout above 60 to 70%, profit and dividend growth above inflation.
4. Estimate profit to the end of the financial year from Codal, with his channel’s template.
5. Forward ratios (P/E, P/S, P/D) and benchmarks (FIS margin, receivables, inventory turnover): better than the market average.
6. Price: the buying range from the Akhza rate and a P/D under 5; buy in steps.
7. Monitor every report; sell on the fundamental stop-loss or on reaching the target; measure every asset with the gold ruler.
Estimating Profit His Way
He shows this method in the video “How to forecast companies’ profit” (Tir 1405) and in his channel’s template.
1. Yearly sales = sales of the reported months ÷ number of months × 12 (“at the current pace”).
2. Take the FIS profit margin from the latest financial statements, without non-recurring items.
3. Add recurring other income (deposit interest, dividends, services); not one-offs like asset sales.
4. Work with the parent company’s statements, not the consolidated ones.
5. If the company’s financial year has changed, build a 12-month profit.
6. The EPS and P/E that tsetmc shows are trailing; build the forward number yourself.
7. If last year’s meeting hasn’t been held yet, subtract the dividend on its way from the market value; the result is the buyer’s real cost (the Shabandar example in the next lesson).
He doesn’t model seasonality: he sets aside businesses whose sales aren’t predictable.
The year’s estimated profit = estimated sales × FIS profit margin + recurring other income
Where He Doesn’t Enter at All
In the video “The investor’s personality traits” (Mehr 1404) he states two “don’t enter” cases plainly: a company under Article 141 and a company with a weak operating profit margin.
The paper doesn’t score loss-making companies or companies whose income can’t be predicted.
An adverse audit report, or one full of qualifications, means the numbers can’t be relied on.

Industry screen: in part six of the mini-course “Financial crisis management” (Mehr 1404) he sets aside industries with an average payout of about 34 to 36%, and pharmaceuticals with a collection period of about 277 days.
He sees receivables at 74% of assets as a sign of low profit quality; the market average is about 33%.
The Price Ceiling, Three Ways

1. From P/E: market-value ceiling = estimated profit × buying P/E. The buying P/E comes from the Akhza rate (1 ÷ rate + about 1). In the video “Everything about stocks in 20 questions” (Tir 1404) he gives a P/E of 4 to 4.5 as the buying benchmark.
2. From P/D: market-value ceiling = estimated profit × two-year average payout × 4.5 to 5 (video “The best financial ratios”).
3. From return: if a stock’s expected return is below about 40%, the interest rate at that time, he goes to gold.
All three say the same thing: a stock must give more than fixed income. The FIS calculator on the Practice tab works out the first two.
He buys in steps so that if the price goes lower, there is still an opportunity.

After buying, recalculate every monthly and quarterly report with the same template.
Fundamental stop-loss: a loss, a falling quarterly profit margin, falling sales. After that: switch to gold or to a stock with a better report.

Method Details 1: Checklist, Estimate, Dollar and Comparison
A “Good Company” in One Breath
In the video “Why is the stock market positive right now?” (Khordad 1405) he runs through the “good company” checklist in one go:
An FIS profit margin above 30%, and better above 40%.
Low receivables to assets; roughly under 15 to 20% (the machine transcript of this part isn’t fully clear).
A payout above 60%, ideally 90%.
A share of exports is a plus, when the company’s dollar rate lags the free-market dollar.
A forward P/E under 4.
The meeting hasn’t been held yet; that is, the dividend is still ahead of you.
In a practical example he shows a 37% margin as good, receivables to assets of 27% as still green, and a 41% payout as “neither good nor bad”.
Correct the Estimate Every Month
In the video “Learning about gold, silver and analysing company reports” (Tir 1405) he builds the year’s profit from the last quarter × 4 (or the average month × 12) and the latest margin.
He also builds the last 12 months’ profit (TTM) himself: last financial year’s profit + this year’s period profit − the same period’s profit last year.
According to him the aim isn’t an exact forecast; it is a sign of the company’s short-term state.
From the yearly number he works out the “monthly sales needed” and measures each monthly report against it. A good report is one that fulfils the analyst’s estimate.
He doesn’t model seasonality: a business whose sales aren’t predictable, selling one quarter and not the next, is no use to him.

Items: asset sales stay out; he doesn’t see currency translation gains as quality, recurring profit and sets them aside to be conservative; deposit interest only if it is likely to repeat (for example, deposits have grown).

Comparison in Four Stages
In the video “Learning to monitor economic and financial markets” (Bahman 1404) he makes comparison a four-stage process:
1. The company itself: the variables first, then valuation.
2. Its place in the industry, by size and profit margin. Between two companies in the same industry, he prefers the higher margin.
3. Companies of the same size across the whole market, by market-value rank on tsetmc.
4. The whole market: TTM P/E, trading value, block trades, mood and risk.
And one behavioural rule: “a good one that got better” is lower risk than “a bad one that got good”.

Buying in Steps His Way
In the video “Dollar income in the stock market” (Shahrivar 1405) he builds the expected dollar profit from the last quarter × 4 and works out the “monthly sales needed” from it.
First step: when the ratios are attractive.
Second step: only when the next monthly report fulfils that sales level and the market value is still below the target value.
He hasn’t said publicly how many steps there are.
He calls a reward-to-risk ratio above 3 “very attractive”.

His own example of the dividend’s effect: buy at a P/E of 4 (price 400, profit 100). You receive 60 in dividends and your cost becomes 340. If next year’s profit is 140, the P/E on your cost is about 2.4.
How Many Stocks? The Market Decides
In the same video he says the number of stocks is decided by the market, not by you: however many pass a tough screen.
His funnel: of about 800 companies, 80 first-rate, 500 ordinary and the rest dangerous; and elsewhere “800, 80, 8”.
To beginners he suggests about 5 to 10 stocks (the machine transcript of this part isn’t fully clear).
The rest of the money stays in gold, silver or cash. His example when good stocks are scarce: 80% gold and 20% stocks.
